title: Ten minutes of focus
hook: put the attention research into one sit

segments.voice: Yesterday, nature restores: a few minutes of looking at trees, and tired attention gets some of its strength back. Did you find a tree to look at? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

A kitchen timer, the cheap kind that ticks, turned to ten. Ten minutes is a cup of coffee going lukewarm on the counter. It's the wait for a late bus. Nobody would call it a long time. And yet ask someone to sit with nothing but their breath for ten minutes, and the clock seems to slow down and fill up with traffic: plans, songs, arguments from last week. Lately this path has been reading the science of attention: the gorilla people didn't see, the brain that idles, the phone on the table, the trees. Today there's no new study. Today all of it goes into one sit.
screen: `A TIMER TURNED TO TEN.` → `THE CLOCK FILLS WITH TRAFFIC.` → `TODAY, ONE SIT.`

segments.voice: First, one object. Researchers who study meditation describe two broad styles: focused attention, which rests on one thing, and open monitoring, which watches whatever comes up. Today is the first kind. The object is the breath, because it's always with you and it's always moving, so there's something to follow. Second, the drift. The resting-brain research described a mind that gets busy the moment it isn't given a job. So expect the mind to leave the breath. That isn't the sit going wrong. The drift is the material the sit is made of. Third, the return. William James, in his Principles of Psychology, wrote about the power of bringing back a wandering attention "over and over again," and he called it the root of judgment, character and will. Notice what he praised. Not attention that never wanders. The bringing back. Each return is one repetition, the way one lift of a weight is one repetition. Fourth, what to count. If ten minutes pass and the mind wandered off again and again, that sit wasn't wasted. It was full of returns. The retreat studies this path looked at reported gains in attention, and they were modest gains, after long practice. So the honest promise of ten minutes isn't a calm, empty mind. It's chance after chance to notice and come back. Calm may show up some days. Some days it won't. The returns are there either way, and the returns are the training.
screen: `ONE OBJECT: THE BREATH.` · `THE DRIFT IS THE MATERIAL.` · then, large: `OVER AND OVER AGAIN.` · then: `COUNT RETURNS, NOT CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the first stretch of ten minutes of focus. Sit so your back is upright and easy. Let your eyes close, or rest them low on the floor. Find the breath where it's clearest for you: the nostrils, the chest or the belly. Stay with that one spot. When you notice you've gone somewhere else, a plan, a tune, a worry, say one quiet word inside, "back," and return to the next breath. No scolding. Every "back" counts as a repetition. When the bell ends, if you have the time, keep sitting on your own until the ten minutes are done. The bell holds the time.
Ten minutes of focus. One object, the breath, and the patient work of bringing attention back to it, again and again. Today's word.

Your line: ten minutes. Today, find ten minutes somewhere, a lunch break, a parked car, the edge of the bed, and give them to the breath. Count returns, not calm. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: People who practice breath meditation may sit for a set time, such as ten minutes, resting attention on the breath and gently returning to it each time the mind wanders; teachers of this style treat each return as the practice itself.
